b1.text: Every second, software makes thousands of small decisions.

b2.text: Which team should get this ticket? Is this prompt a jailbreak? How urgent is this email?

b3.text: None of these are open questions. Each has a small, known set of answers, and that shape of problem deserves its own kind of model.

b4.text: Meet System 1 decision engines: models that answer typed questions in a single forward pass, with a probability for every allowed answer.

b5.text: Our reference implementation is Laya, an open-source, multilingual decision engine.

b1.text: Today, the default is to ask a large language model.

b2.text: It writes the answer one token at a time. Then your code parses the text, checks the label is one you allowed, and retries when it isn't.

b3.text: A full generation, a parser and a retry path, for a decision with only three possible answers.

b1.text: The name comes from Daniel Kahneman's Thinking, Fast and Slow, which describes two modes of thought.

b2.text: System 1 is fast, automatic and cheap: recognizing a face, sensing that a sentence is hostile.

b3.text: System 2 is slow, deliberate and expensive: long multiplication, checking an argument.

b4.text: Software has the same split. Language models made System 2 cheap enough to use everywhere, but most production decisions are still System 1 work: known options, on every request, where speed and consistency matter most.

b5.text: So the fast system should answer first, and its confidence should decide when to call in the slow one.

b2.text: An autoregressive model generates its answer token by token. Each token is another sequential forward pass, and the output can be malformed, or a label you never offered.

b3.text: A decision engine never writes the label. The options are part of its input. One forward pass scores every option side by side, and a softmax turns those scores into a distribution over exactly those options.

b4.text: So the answer is always valid. Every option gets a probability, so you see how close the runner-up was. And the cost doesn't depend on the answer.

b1.text: Every decision is expressed with three question types.

b2.text: Choice picks one label from several, like which department should handle a request. The label descriptions are what the model actually matches against.

b3.text: Score places the input on an ordered scale, like urgency, and returns the expected level: a probability-weighted average of the levels.

b4.text: And noul returns the probability that a statement is true. Is this phishing? Does the user threaten to cancel?

b5.text: Several questions about the same input are answered together, in one batched call.

b1.text: Inside, each question becomes one row of tokens.

b2.text: A header with the question type and instructions. Then every option, each preceded by a mask token that marks where its score will be read. Then the input itself.

b3.text: The encoder is bidirectional, so each marker sees its option, the question, the rival options and the input, all at once.

b4.text: But the options share one fixed token budget. With seventy-seven options, each label keeps about three tokens, and similar labels collapse into the same text. The rule of thumb: keep choice questions under about twenty options.

b1.text: Now follow that row through the model.

b2.text: A pretrained encoder, ModernBERT large for English, reads the whole row. A type embedding says which primitive this is, and a small two-layer decision head refines every position.

b3.text: The model gathers the hidden vector at each marker, and a shared scorer turns each one into a single number: one logit per option.

b4.text: Because options are inputs, not fixed output units, the same weights can score two options or twenty, even labels the model has never seen.

b5.text: On a Tesla T4, one question takes about thirty-three milliseconds on the multilingual checkpoint. Ten questions take seventy-two: about seven milliseconds each.

b1.text: Decoding is a few lines: divide the logits by a temperature, then apply a softmax.

b2.text: Temperature never changes which option wins. It only changes how confident the model sounds.

b3.text: And of the two confidence numbers the engine reports, gate on answer confidence, the probability of the chosen answer. That's the number calibration is fitted on.

b1.text: For those probabilities to mean anything, honesty has to be trained in.

b2.text: The tool is a strictly proper scoring rule: a reward that is maximized, on average, only by reporting what you truly believe.

b3.text: If the truth is seventy percent, the log, spherical and Brier scores all peak at exactly seventy. A linear reward keeps climbing towards certainty: it pays for overconfidence. And plain accuracy can't tell fifty-one percent from ninety-nine.

b1.text: Laya's training method builds on this. It's called RLCD: Reinforcement Learning for Calibrated Decisions.

b2.text: For each item, it adds noise to the logits to sample a small group of candidate distributions, rewards each with a proper scoring rule, and compares it with its group's average.

b3.text: The logits move towards the above-average samples, while a soft cross-entropy term pulls towards the teacher's full distribution, uncertainty included.

b4.text: Fine-tuning is where the accuracy comes from. On the typed-decisions benchmark, the base model scores zero point three six. Fine-tuned, it reaches zero point seven seven, above the teacher's own self-agreement.

b1.text: A model is calibrated when its confidence means what it says: of the answers given at eighty percent, about eighty percent are right.

b2.text: The shipped checkpoints are over-confident. The fix is temperature scaling, fitted on held-out data. It never changes an answer, and it cuts calibration error from zero point four seven to zero point zero eight.

b3.text: But calibration can't rescue an input the model cannot read. On Khmer, the English checkpoint scored zero accuracy, at ninety-five percent confidence.

b1.text: That's why Laya ships three checkpoints and a router.

b2.text: One for English, a faster multilingual one for over a hundred languages, and one fine-tuned for four specific workflows.

b3.text: Before any forward pass, the router detects script and language in well under a millisecond, and sends the text to a checkpoint that can read it. Across fifty-one languages, usable coverage nearly doubles: from twenty-three to forty-five.

b1.text: In production, a decision engine returns evidence, not permission.

b2.text: The core pattern is confidence gating: above a threshold, act automatically; below it, escalate to a human, a rule, or a larger model. The threshold is a policy, chosen from measured accuracy and the cost of mistakes.

b3.text: Roll out in stages: shadow, compare, choose a policy, then promote a bounded slice of traffic, with a rollback plan.

b2.text: An agent loop is full of small, typed decisions. Is this input safe? Which tool comes next? Is the task done? Is this output good enough to send?

b3.text: System 1 takes those in milliseconds, and hands only the uncertain cases to System 2.

b4.text: In one browser agent, fine-tuning lifted the right-element choice from ten percent, which is chance, to nearly two thirds, with each step decided in about twenty milliseconds.

b1.text: It isn't magic, and the limits deserve plain words.

b2.text: A decision engine is not a reasoner: it can't explain itself or answer open questions. Zero-shot, the base checkpoints are near chance on specialized workflows, they ship over-confident, and long option lists or other languages need care.

b3.text: So evaluate on your own traffic, fine-tune on your own decisions, fit temperatures on held-out data, and gate every change in CI.

b1.text: Let System 1 answer first: in one pass, with honest probabilities.

b2.text: And let calibrated confidence decide when it's time to think slow.
